Keywords: Cuban, For, Especially

outputs.L1:
To cure myself of longing for Cuban songs, I wrote a Cuban song about the need for people to suppress their fantasies, especially unhealthy ones. The song begins with a reference to the sea, because the sea is like a need so vast and deep that it can never be swallowed.

It then explores common myths about the Cuban people and their folklore: the story of a little Carib boy mistakenly abandoned to the sea; the legend of a bird who desired song so desperately that he surrendered flight; and the tale of a queen whose strength surpassed that of a rival king.

The song continues with reflections on morality, followed by a line about the sea—how deep it is, how many creatures depend upon its nourishment, and how beautiful it is to need.

The song is ending now because I can no longer bear to hear it. I call this song of needful love my voice.
outputs.L2: I composed a song in the Cuban style to rid myself of my longing for Cuban music. Its subject was the importance of restraining desire, particularly when those desires are harmful. It opened with the ocean, whose immense depth resembles a hunger too vast ever to be satisfied. From there, it examined familiar legends and beliefs associated with Cuba and its folklore: a young Carib boy accidentally left to drift at sea; a bird so eager to sing that it surrendered its ability to fly; and a queen more powerful than the king who opposed her. The song then turned to questions of right and wrong before returning to the ocean—its unfathomable depths, the countless beings sustained by it, and the beauty contained in needing. Now the music draws to a close because I can no longer endure listening to it. This song about love filled with longing is what I call my voice.
outputs.L3:
The speaker writes a Cuban song in an effort to overcome an intense longing for Cuban music. At the same time, the song becomes a way of arguing that unhealthy fantasies should be resisted or suppressed rather than allowed to take control. This conflict between desire and restraint shapes the work as a whole.

At the center of the song is the sea, which symbolizes an immense and ultimately unfulfillable need. Its vastness suggests a longing that cannot be contained or fully satisfied. To explore this longing, the speaker draws on Cuban myth and folklore, invoking the story of an abandoned Carib boy, a bird that gives up flight in exchange for song, and a queen whose strength surpasses that of a rival king. These figures embody different forms of loss, sacrifice, endurance, and power.

The song also reflects on morality, asking how desire should be understood and whether it ought to be restrained. Yet need is not portrayed as purely destructive. It can nourish the imagination, generate beauty, and give rise to art, even as it causes suffering. Eventually, however, the emotional force of the song becomes unbearable. The speaker brings it to an end and identifies this expression of longing—this love shaped by need—as their own true voice.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins by trying to resist a powerful longing for Cuban songs. Rather than surrendering directly to that desire, the speaker attempts to control it through composition, creating a new song that can contain and examine the longing. This creative act is therefore both an expression of need and an effort to suppress it. The song becomes a space in which the speaker can question whether desire is nourishing or destructive, especially when it grows so intense that it threatens emotional balance.

Images of the sea give this conflict its central form. The sea evokes Cuba, distance, memory, and the dangerous force of appetite. It can sustain life, connect separated places, and carry music across boundaries, but it can also overwhelm, consume, and drown. Through this imagery, the speaker presents longing as something similarly double-edged: it draws the self toward beauty and belonging while also exposing the self to pain. The sea’s constant motion suggests that desire cannot simply be silenced. Even when resisted, it returns in waves.

Cuban myths and folklore deepen the song’s exploration of longing. These inherited stories connect the speaker’s private need to a larger cultural memory, suggesting that desire is not merely an individual weakness. It belongs to a history, a community, and a tradition of storytelling and music. At the same time, the moral elements of these tales warn against unhealthy forms of wanting. Appetite can become obsession, and the pursuit of what is absent can lead to suffering or self-destruction. The speaker uses folklore not only to celebrate Cuban culture but also to judge and test the longing that culture awakens.

Yet the attempt to discipline desire gradually reveals a contradiction. The speaker can criticize need only by creating a song from it. The very longing that causes pain also supplies the material, energy, and emotional urgency necessary for artistic expression. What first appears to be a dangerous hunger proves to be sustaining as well: it connects the speaker to memory, culture, and imagination. Without that need, there would be no song.

By the end, the composition has become more than an imitation of the Cuban songs the speaker misses. It has become the speaker’s own voice. The longing cannot be separated from creativity because it is the force that makes creativity possible. Although need remains painful and potentially unhealthy, it is also profound, enduring, and life-giving. The song therefore does not resolve the conflict by eliminating desire. Instead, it accepts that desire and art are inseparable: the wound of longing is also the source from which the speaker’s voice emerges.
outputs.L5: Cuban culture is known for its vibrant music, colorful art, and flavorful cuisine. For travelers seeking warmth and energy, Cuba offers an unforgettable experience. It is especially famous for salsa dancing, classic cars, beautiful beaches, and dishes such as ropa vieja, rice, and black beans.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about suppressing the desire for Cuban songs, using the sea, folklore, morality, and “needful love” as recurring motifs.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep the radio dark at dusk  
when the sea begins rehearsing  
its blue morality against the stones.

No trumpets.  
No clave lifting its small, bright ladder.  
No voice from Havana  
turning sorrow into a door.

I tell myself restraint is a clean room,  
a white shirt buttoned to the throat.  
I tell myself folklore is only smoke—  
the fisherman married to the moon,  
the saint disguised as a beggar,  
the drowned horse galloping home  
beneath the sea.

Still, the rhythm finds the window.

It enters without music:  
in the spoon against the cup,  
in rain knocking three times,  
in my pulse, that faithless drummer  
asking for needful love.

What is morality  
but the name we give the shore  
when we are afraid to swim?

I fold my hands.  
I do not hum.  
I place each forbidden melody  
under the tongue  
like a coin for the ferryman.

But folklore warns me:  
what is buried learns roots;  
what is silenced grows wings;  
what is denied returns barefoot,  
salt-haired, laughing.

The sea knows this.  
All night it repeats  
its one enormous song  
and calls repetition mercy.

I answer with silence.  
I answer with morality.  
I answer: no, not tonight,  
not that guitar, not that bronze cry,  
not the streets flowering in percussion.

Yet needful love  
is needful love—  
a hunger with no court of appeal,  
a lantern smuggled through the ribs.

So I stand at the edge of the sea,  
guarding myself from Cuba,  
from folklore, from drums,  
from the beautiful crime of remembering,

while far inside me  
an island refuses obedience,

and every wave  
comes ashore singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal prose poem in which the speaker cures an obsession by writing a Cuban song they eventually cannot bear to hear.
counterfactuals.output:
I cured myself of you by writing a Cuban song.

First I built it a small guitar from the ribs of a blue marlin. Then I taught the strings to remember Havana at dusk: balconies sweating sugar, taxis bright as bitten lemons, the sea combing its green hair with a fork of lightning. Into the chorus I poured every hour I had spent orbiting your silence. The hours turned to rum. The silence put on white shoes and began to dance.

A trumpet entered through the kitchen window carrying a red handkerchief. Behind it came the claves—two little bones knocking at the door of the dead. I gave the song your mouth, but not your name. I gave it my fever, but not my bed. By morning, the congas had driven your shadow from the walls, and my heart, that stubborn island, had slipped its chain and floated calmly into the Gulf.

The cure was complete. I ate mangoes without thinking of your shoulders. I watched rain without expecting you to emerge from it. Even the moon, once your accomplice, returned my letters unopened.

But the song escaped.

It traveled in the throats of strangers, in dented radios, in cafés where ceiling fans slowly beheaded the smoke. Children whistled it to their kites. Old men played it on porches while dominoes clicked like teeth. Each time I heard it, the trumpet lifted its red handkerchief, and the sea inside me stood up.

Now, when the first chord finds me, I cover my ears. Not because I love you still, but because I do not. The song has kept the body of my obsession perfectly preserved, dancing barefoot in a room I have survived.

Some nights it plays from a passing car, sweet and unbearable, and all of Havana pours through the keyhole—rum, thunder, salt, your vanished face—while I stand on the other side, cured, weeping, and wait for the music to go away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in loose blank verse that describes its own composition. Include a Carib boy abandoned at sea, a bird that sacrifices flight for song, a powerful queen, and reflections on unhealthy fantasies.
counterfactuals.output:
I set the first line loose upon the tide,  
then watch it drift beyond the reach of rhyme.  
A Carib boy clings to a splintered mast,  
abandoned where the sea erases names.  
I give him clouds, but clouds are only ink;  
I give him land, then cross the word away.  

Above him wheels a small, bright-throated bird.  
It folds its wings and lets the currents pass,  
choosing the weight of music over sky.  
Its song becomes the measure of these lines,  
each note a feather fastened to the page,  
each silence where the power of flight was lost.  

Now comes the queen, and with her comes a throne  
carved from the dark wood at the poem’s edge.  
She lifts one hand; the waves compose themselves.  
She lifts the other; armies turn to reeds.  
I almost make her merciful, then stop.  
Power prefers a mirror to a heart.  

The boy looks up. The bird sings from the mast.  
The queen regards them through a crown of fire.  
And I, who made this peril for their sake,  
begin to doubt the hunger of the scene:  
the sweet, unhealthy wish to suffer grandly,  
to be the chosen ruin, loved by fate,  
to call obsession vision, wounds a proof,  
and loneliness a kingdom of the mind.  

So I revise. The fire becomes dawn.  
The throne is only driftwood on the sand.  
The queen steps down, still powerful, still feared,  
and wades waist-deep to pull the boy ashore.  
The bird, its wings forgotten, keeps its song.  

This poem builds the beach beneath their feet,  
then leaves its final footprints incomplete.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a self-referential literary poem about longing and repression, where the sea symbolizes an immense, uncontainable need and the final song becomes the speaker’s voice.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Poem Keeps the Tide**

I wrote the sea as if a word could hold it—  
four letters, a small blue lock—  
then watched the page grow wet around me,  
its margins darkening like cuffs.

All night I practiced being quiet.  
I folded each desire into a bird  
and shut it in the ribs. By morning  
the room was full of wings I would not name.

Do not mistake restraint for absence.  
Beneath this line, another line is breaking;  
beneath my tongue, the black waves shoulder  
their immeasurable weight toward shore.

I tried to end the poem with a harbor,  
a lamp, a hand withdrawing from the glass.  
But longing has no grammar for enough.  
It floods the sentence meant to keep it still.

So let the final song unfasten me.  
Let every barred syllable become foam,  
every hush widen into water—

I am no longer singing of the sea.

The sea is singing.

The song is my mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a melancholic narrative poem inspired by Cuban folklore and music, exploring desire, myth, morality, and the paradoxical beauty of needing something.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Bolero for the Thirsting Man**

In Matanzas, where the moon combs silver  
through the sugarcane’s black hair,  
a fisherman named Tomás heard singing  
beneath the river’s skin.

It was not the river calling,  
though rivers are lonely and call to everyone.  
It was not a woman, though the song  
wore a woman’s sorrow like perfume.

The old men playing dominoes warned him:  
*That is the güije in the reeds.*  
The women crossing themselves whispered:  
*That is Yemayá counting her drowned.*  
His mother struck the table once and said,  
*Whatever names you in the dark, don’t answer.*

But desire is a drum with one command.

Each night the clave knocked within him—  
two strokes for hunger, three for hope—  
and from a courtyard a tres guitar  
stitched gold thread through the heat.

Tomás had a wife named Inés  
whose hands smelled of coffee and ironed linen.  
She loved him with the daily mercy  
of beans kept warm beneath a plate,  
of sandals placed beside the bed,  
of silence when the money failed.

Still, the river sang.

It promised neither flesh nor fortune.  
It promised only that somewhere  
his life had another life inside it,  
blue, impossible, without a shore.

So Tomás began to leave small offerings:  
a coin, a cigar, white flowers,  
one spoonful of rum trembling  
in a chipped enamel cup.

The town called this devotion.  
His mother called it vanity.  
Inés called it nothing at all,  
and that was the name that wounded most.

One midnight, dressed in his wedding shirt,  
Tomás followed the bolero downstream.  
The ceiba trees lifted their roots  
like saints unwilling to intervene.

At the river mouth, the sea opened—  
vast as a mother’s forgiveness,  
cruel as a mother who knows  
forgiveness cannot save her child.

There, on a rock, sat the singer:  
not maiden, spirit, fish, nor god,  
but a mirror made of water  
holding the face he had at seventeen.

“Come,” said the life he had not lived.

Behind him, faintly, the village breathed:  
Inés turning in their narrow bed,  
his mother waking without reason,  
the dominoes clicking like small bones.

Tomás stepped forward.

Then stopped.

For he understood the oldest curse:  
we do not always want the thing itself—  
sometimes we want the wanting,  
that bright wound proving we are alive.

He wept until dawn salted the bay.  
Then he poured the rum into the tide  
and walked home carrying his hunger  
as carefully as a candle.

Inés opened the door.

She did not forgive him.  
She moved aside.

And in that narrow mercy  
he saw what the sea could never offer:  
love was not the end of needing,  
nor virtue the death of desire.

Love was the bowl left empty  
so another might choose to fill it;  
the unanswered chord in every song,  
beautiful because it must resolve—

and more beautiful still  
because it never does.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
